utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber received a waiver signed by Mr. Mladic that he waives his right to be present in court today. I take it that that will be filed if it is not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Therefore, we'll proceed in the absence of the accused. I move to another development, which is that the Chamber was informed that the witness who was expected to be back at 9.30 this morning left this country shortly after midnight and invites the parties to make written submissions as to how to proceed under those circumstances, and we'd like to receive those submissions by Friday, close of business.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we may, we already have other filing deadlines for Friday, and this is a rather novel issue. Can we at least have until Monday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although you have some extra time perhaps today, but the Chamber nevertheless is willing to give you until Monday but then 9.00 in the morning, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, if the deadline is changed that would, of course, be for the Prosecution as well. We just discussed for a second whether it would be appropriate to first hear from the Defence and then from the Prosecution, but the Chamber considers it appropriate that both parties give their input, not necessarily the one responding to the other. And if there will be any follow-up, then that's still possible. Then I think under present circumstances -- but let me just confer for a second with Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, in the present circumstances, there's no need for Russian interpretation any further. Therefore, the Chamber would wish to thank the Russian interpreters for their assistance provided during the last two days, and the interpreters are excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll say a few more words about the present situation, the absence of the witness. Then I'll deal with some rather, perhaps to some extent, boring procedural matters. And at the very end, the Chamber will say a few words about scheduling in the near future. So let me start with Witness Demurenko. Under normal circumstances once a statement is admitted, of course, the Chamber would decide on the associated exhibits as well. We'll not do that at this very moment, and the parties are invited to include in their written submissions what to do with the associated exhibits, if they consider it appropriate to receive any evidence at all. And then we'll deal with that later. Then quite a number - it's my estimate - that it will take some 35, 40 minutes to read most of the decisions. I'll try to do it not too quickly. And I'll start with a decision on the Defence renewed bar table submission in relation to 65 ter number 1D02597. On the 18th of January, the Defence filed its fifth bar table motion tendering into evidence, inter alia, the document bearing Rule 65 ter number 1D02597, a bulletin from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which provides information about an alleged attack on the 20th of October, 1993 in Sarajevo. On the 1st of March, the Prosecution responded not opposing its admission, subject to the Defence providing a complete English translation. On 30th of May, the Chamber issued its decision, denying admission without prejudice. On the 10th of June, the Defence filed a renewed bar table motion re-tendering the document with a complete translation. The Chamber finds that the document is relevant to the Sarajevo component of the case, observes that it is stamped, and considers that it bears sufficient indicia of reliability and authenticity for the purpose of admission. The Chamber also considers that the Defence has set out with sufficient clarity and specificity how the document would fit into its case. Pursuant to Rule 89(C), the Chamber admits the document into evidence and gives the Prosecution, if there's any remaining issue, a week to revisit the matter. I see that there's some -- that's perhaps about the complete translation, which is not available for a long time to the Prosecution. I can read face expressions. I see that there's at least some -- Mr. Tieger, Mr. Weber, Mr. Traldi, your faces are ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. President. I can't alert you to a specific issue now. We'll rise if it's appropriate shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As always, and since we are in court now, and since the translation has been received only very recently, the Chamber decides already on admission but allows the Prosecution to revisit the matter within one week. Mr. Registrar, for 65 ter 1D02597, what would the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D2124, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D2124 is admitted into evidence. I now move to a decision on the Defence renewed bar table submission as to Rule 65 ter 1D02541. On the 18th of January of this year, the Defence filed its fifth bar table motion tendering into evidence, inter alia, the document bearing Rule 65 ter number 1D02541, a bulletin from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which provides information about the treatment of Serbs in ABiH-held territory. On the 1st of March, the Prosecution responded, opposing its admission because only brief portions of the original were translated into English. On the 30th of May, the Chamber issued its decision denying without prejudice the admission of this document. On the 10th of June, the Defence filed a renewed bar table submission re-tendering this document with a complete translation. The Chamber finds that the document is relevant to the Sarajevo component of the case, observes that it's stamped, and considers that it bears sufficient indicia of reliability and authenticity for the purpose of admission. The Chamber also considers that the Defence has set out with sufficient clarity and specificity how the document would fit into its case. Pursuant to Rule 89(C), the Chamber admits the document into evidence. The Prosecution, since the full translation is available only since the 10th of June, has one week to revisit the matter if need be. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, on this one we have checked the translation and it's acceptable to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the week is over for you. No further time will be given to the Prosecution to revisit the matter. Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2125 Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D2125 is admitted into evidence. I now move to Rule 65 ter 12990a. On the 18th of January, the Defence filed its fourth bar table motion tendering into evidence, inter alia, the document bearing Rule 65 ter number 12990, an extract from a book entitled "Wartime Letters of Radovan Karadzic," published by the International Committee for the Truth About Radovan Karadzic, in Belgrade, in 2004. On 23rd of May, 2016, the Trial Chamber issued its decision denying admission on the basis of insufficient indicia of reliability and authenticity. The Chamber found that the document appeared to be a reproduction of a letter type-signed by Radovan Karadzic, bearing no official stamps or signatures, in a book extract that was neither sourced nor named. On the 8th of June of this year, the Defence filed a renewed bar table motion requesting admission and uploading a new version of the document, bearing Rule 65 ter number 12990a, which incorporates information on the document's provenance. On the 10th of June, the Prosecution responded indicating that it no longer objected to the admission of the document. The Chamber is satisfied that the newly uploaded version of the document provides sufficient information on its provenance and finds that it is relevant and of probative value for the purpose of its admission into evidence. The Chamber also finds that the Defence has set out with sufficient clarity and specificity how the documents would fit into its case. The Chamber therefore admits the document bearing Rule 65 ter number 12990a into evidence pursuant to Rule 89(C) of the Rules. Mr. Registrar, the number to be assigned would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D2126, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D2126 is admitted. I now move to 65 ter 1D05719. On the 9th of June, the Chamber, in its decision on the Defence motion to admit into evidence Subotic and Poparic's expert reports and related documents, indicated that it would deny admission into evidence of the document bearing Rule 65 ter number 1D05719, a photograph of a monument. The disposition of the decision erroneously referenced the document as being admitted into evidence. The Chamber clarifies that the document is denied admission into evidence. I now move to a renewed request for the admission of Rule 65 ter number 1D05915a. On the 2nd of June of this year, in its second Defence case omnibus decision, the Chamber denied the admission into evidence of a video bearing Rule 65 ter number 1D05915a without prejudice. This was because the Defence had not provided the Chamber with a copy of the video. On the 6th of June, a copy of the video was made available to the Chamber. On the 7th of June, the Defence filed a motion requesting that the video be admitted into evidence. Given that the video was initially tendered in a joint submission, the Chamber understands that the Prosecution does not object to the admission of the video. The video concerns alleged shelling incidents in Sarajevo as charged in the indictment and contains clips from news reports. A still from the video was put to witness Zorica Subotic in court on the 30th of September, 2015. Under these circumstances, the Chamber admits Rule 65 ter number 1D05915a into evidence. And, Mr. Registrar, what number would be assigned to this video?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D2127, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D2127. I now move to D2022 and D2086. On the 8th of June, the Chamber admitted these two exhibits into evidence and instructed the Defence to upload into e-court English translations that match the B/C/S originals of both documents. On the 14th of June, the Defence informed the Chamber and the Prosecution, via e-mail, that it had uploaded the revised translations into e-court. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to: Replace the existing translation of Exhibit D2022 with the revised and reduced translation uploaded under doc ID 1D31-1020; and Replace the existing translation of Exhibit D2086 with the revised translation uploaded under doc ID 1D31-1021. I now move to the decision on Defence renewed bar table submissions as to Rule 65 ter numbers 1D03471 and 1D05966. On the 18th of January, the Defence filed its fifth bar table motion tendering into evidence, inter alia, the document bearing Rule 65 ter number 1D03471, a document containing excerpts of information on paramilitary groups operating in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Defence also noted that the document, and I quote: "Appears to be an annex to UN Security Council document." On the 1st of March, the Prosecution responded not opposing its admission. On the 30th of May, the Chamber issued its decision denying admission without prejudice on the basis that the document did not bear sufficient indicia of authenticity and reliability. On the 13th of June, the Defence filed a renewed bar table motion re-tendering the document under the same 65 ter number as well as the document bearing 65 ter number 1D05966. The Defence submits that the Prosecution has confirmed that both documents are official documents received from the UN. The document bearing Rule 65 ter number 1D03471 is a preliminary version of the report received from the UN Commission of Experts, and the document bearing 65 ter number 1D05966 is the public version of the report and a UN Security Council document. The Chamber finds that both documents are relevant to the Sarajevo component of the case and further observes that the Defence has demonstrated sufficient indicia of reliability and authenticity for the purpose of admission into evidence. The Chamber also considers that the Defence has set out with sufficient clarity and specificity how the documents would fit into its case. Pursuant to Rule 89(C), the Chamber admits both documents into evidence. And, Mr. Registrar, invites you to assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D03471 will be Exhibit D2128. And 65 ter 1D05966 will be Exhibit D2129.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D2128 and D2129 are admitted into evidence. And if there's any problem remaining, the Prosecution has one week to revisit the matter. I move to the Chamber's decision on Defence renewed bar table submission as to 65 ter 1D02644. On the 18th of January, the Defence filed its fifth bar table motion tendering into evidence, inter alia, the document bearing Rule 65 ter number 1D02644, an ABiH statement from Nihad Hodzic dated 2nd of November, 1993, concerning the alleged actions of ABiH forces in and around Sarajevo during the indictment period. On the 1st of March, the Prosecution responded opposing its admission because the Defence only provided a partial English translation. The Prosecution also noted that the statement related to the document bearing Rule 65 ter number 1D02642, an ABiH special report dated the 6th of June, 1993, which was admitted into evidence on the 30th of May as Exhibit D1792. On the 30th of May, the Chamber issued its decision, denying admission without prejudice. On the 13th of June, the Defence filed a renewed bar table motion re-tendering the document with a complete translation under the same 65 ter number. The Chamber finds that the document is relevant to the Sarajevo component of the case and further observes that it bears sufficient indicia of reliability and authenticity for the purpose of admission into evidence, including signatures. The Chamber also considers that the Defence has set out with sufficient clarity and specificity how the document would fit into its case. Pursuant to Rule 89(C), the Chamber admits the document into evidence. And invites you, Mr. Registrar, to assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D2130, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D2130 is admitted into evidence. And, as always, the Prosecution has one week to revisit the matter if there's any need to do so. Next item is a decision on Defence renewed bar table submission as to 65 ter 1D02958. On the 18th of January, the Defence filed its fifth bar table motion tendering into evidence, inter alia, the document bearing Rule 65 ter number 1D02958, a portion of a 13 August 1994 UNPROFOR report concerning Sarajevo. On the 1st of March, the Prosecution responded not opposing admission, subject to the Defence uploading into e-court the entire document. On the 30th of May, the Chamber issued its decision, denying admission without prejudice. On the 10th of June, the Defence filed a renewed bar table motion re-tendering the complete version of the document under the same Rule 65 ter number. The Chamber finds that the document is relevant to the Sarajevo component of the case and observes that it bears sufficient indicia of reliability and authenticity for admission into evidence, including a stamp, signature, and information regarding the author and recipient. The Chamber also considers that the Defence has set out with sufficient clarity and specificity how the document would fit into its case. Pursuant to Rule 89(C), the Chamber admits the document into evidence. And invites you, Mr. Registrar, to assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D2131, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D2131 is admitted into evidence. Since the full version was only filed, I think, on the 10th of June, if there's any need to revisit the matter, the Prosecution has got a week to do so. These were the rather administrative matters. I would now briefly turn to scheduling. As matters stand now -- of course, with the uncertainty of the developments of today, but as matters stand now it seems that the in-court presentation of Defence evidence is complete, again, with this caveat, that we have two issues pending. The first is absence of Mr. Demurenko today, and the other one is the submissions still to be expected this Friday on another witness and whether and how we could receive the evidence of that other witness. You're on your feet Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We're still expecting, I believe two -- pardon me, two decisions from the Chamber as to documents that the Chamber had ruled should be brought in through a witness. And depending on the decision on those motions that we have filed, of course, those witnesses in question might need to be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- we'll see how that further develops. It's only -- I'm looking at the situation as it appears now, and as I said before there are a few matters of uncertainty which may or may not change the situation. But however that develops, the Chamber will formally close the Defence case once it has decided on all evidentiary motions, and that includes the ones you referred to, and, of course, any follow-up would be considered. Once the Defence case has formally been closed, there will be a possibility for rebuttal and rejoinder evidence to be presented, and the Chamber will set the deadline for the final briefs in due course. However, I wish to remind the parties that they were already advised informally that the deadline could be the 1st of September, 2016, and the Chamber has emphasised again and again that any delays in hearing evidence in court should not be understood as that there was more time to prepare for the final briefs, that the time should be used even if not every evidentiary issue had been finally settled. There is a fair chance that we would not have a hearing soon. Is there any matter the parties would like to raise at this very moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, we had considered raising the timing and extent or duration of the closing arguments. I can tell you we've had discussions with Defence about that noting, in particular, the correspondence and guidance we relied upon in comparison with the Karadzic case for determining the size of the final brief, and so we settled on an agreed proposal for that. And, well, one thing we can do, I suppose, is communicate informally with the Chambers about that when the deadline for the final brief is formally set. I think that's -- I'm seeing Mr. Ivetic nod. I think he's -- it's just a question of how we communicate this to you, but I think the timing would be more appropriate since it is linked to a date, if we did so, after we had the date formally set for the deadline of the final brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I see no problem with identifying the time-period between the actual filing date and -- that -- we can do that I think, and then we can all do the math based upon the date, sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have agreed on it. Apparently I take it that you have a number of days or weeks or months, I wouldn't think about years, after the final briefs have been submitted. If you could inform the Chamber on how many days or weeks or months that would be now already so that we would have an indication by way of a joint submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Happy to do so. The date we -- the date we selected jointly or agreed upon was appropriate, working from the September 1st date, was October 10th. In part, because of the day of the week on which September 1st fell. But the idea was roughly five weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in terms of the length of argument, we discussed the fact that in the Karadzic case ten hours were allotted for each side, but that was -- and -- but given the length of time we can sit on a given day or in -- in continuity for each session, it's very clear that that would encompass three courtroom days, and there's no way to -- whether it's nine hours or ten hours or ten and a half hours, whatever it was in that area, so we consider just to propose three days for each -- each party. And, finally, with respect to rebuttal and surrebuttal. In Karadzic, that was an hour and a half for each side, and we would also suggest that there be at least one courtroom day in between the end of closing and the commencement of rebuttal. But since rebuttal is an hour and a half, obviously the rebuttal and surrebuttal would take place in the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused. You said in Karadzic rebuttal and surrebuttal one hour and a half. For each side we would also suggest that there be at least one courtroom day in -- oh, between the end of the closing and the commencement of rebuttal. So, yes, I do understand. You do it on one day but you'd like to have one day in between the -- [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I say a courtroom day. Obviously if the closing ended on a Thursday, then that would be -- that issue would be mooted by virtue of the calendar days if it elapsed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. Mr. Ivetic, we can consider this as a joint submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay, is there any ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just have a look. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm advised that there is one additional bar table submission that appears not to have been mentioned in the course of the motions raised by the Bench so far, and that relates to exhibit 1D032854 [sic]. I simply wanted to alert the Court to the fact that we did not object to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask to check that number. We don't have 1D numbers that high, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, usually it is after the zero there are following four digits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just repeat the number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we are within the range of the numbers used [Overlapping speakers] ... --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... because that's what I saw on my screen as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's hereby on the record that the Prosecution does not oppose that motion. Most likely we'll then deliver a short written decision on the matter, but that's hereby on the record. Any other matter to be raised at this very moment? Nothing. Then we will adjourn, sine die. We stand adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.28 a.m.,
